Is anyone interested in a tactic able to rapidly compute Bernoulli numbers? By "compute" I mean showing that a given Bernoulli number is what it is (Pari/GP or python can compute those very fast).

I don't want to go super far, for example getting to the 100-th would already be enough. To give an idea it is

-94598037819122125295227433069493721872702841533066936133385696204311395415197247711/33330

Currently what I did is the following

def bernoulliCompute (n : ℕ) : ℚ :=
  ... --something computable that is more or less the definition

theorem bernoulliCompute_eq (n : ℕ) : bernoulliCompute n = bernoulli n := by
 ...

And then I wrote a small tactic that wraps things things together, without doing anything fancy.

Maybe @Bhavik Mehta ?

Maybe an LLM or a human could port into Lean the first ever computer program, written by Ada Lovelace, which did just that! Would be a very cool project (seriously).

Although I think things moved on a bit since 1843; probably a good place to start with modern algorithms is the Buhler-Crandall-Ernvall-Metsänkylä paper https://www.jstor.org/stable/2152942?seq=1 , although the actual algorithm will probably be in one of the references.

Related work: "Verifying an Efficient Algorithm for Computing Bernoulli Numbers" by Eberl and Lammich
https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol352-itp2025/LIPIcs.ITP.2025.35/LIPIcs.ITP.2025.35.pdf

With the assistance of claude I wrote a pretty naive implementation and I able to verify that 37 divides the numerator of the 32-th bernoulli number (something relevant for number theoretic applications), and it's already reasonably fast.

Eberl-Lammich: Oh excellent! This beats the 1990 work: the reference for the 2008 algorithm is https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.1347. One of the insights of both these modern algorithms is that it's actually to compute mod p for lots of primes p and then glue the results together using the Chinese Remainder Theorem. This is an important tool in computational number theory but would add an extra layer of complexity to the Lean code. Of course as Kevin points out it's already done in Isabelle/HOL :-)

When we were working on Bernoulli numbers at Imperial the definitions were half-written with computation in mind. Is docs#bernoulli' not computable? I thought we could do fast rational number arithmetic -- or is it just fast integer arithmetic?
They are computable in the sense that eval bernoulli 4 gives the correct answer. But I want a proof that bernoulli 4 = - 1 / 30 and decide doesn't work.

This is pari-gp implementing Lovelace's algorithm (which is the algorithm we already have!) (actually I think I'm wrong -- this algorithm is simpler than Lovelace's) and it gets to 100 in 8ms.

? \\ b(0)=1
? \\ and pari-gp has one-based matrices
? b=vector(101,i,1);
? for(n=1,100,b[n+1]=1-sum(k=0,n-1,binomial(n,k)/(n-k+1)*b[k+1]))
? ##
  ***   last result: cpu time 8 ms, real time 8 ms.
? b[101]

Getting up to a million is kind of a research project for a computer science undergraduate, getting up to 100 is a nice challenge for Lean just evaluating the definition we have. What exactly do you want to do?

Let's say a proof of the following

import Mathlib

example : bernoulli 100 = -94598037819122125295227433069493721872702841533066936133385696204311395415197247711/33330 := by
  sorry

I don't know how to do this in Lean (but see above for how to do it in pari) but one trick is "don't compute BnB_nBn​ more than once" and I'm not sure you need any more tricks to get to B100B_{100}B100​ if pari can do it in 8ms. We just need to be able to add up rationals quickly. Can we?
Yes, this is more or less what I am already doing.

The key definition in Lean is

def bernoulli' (n : ℕ) : ℚ :=
  1 - ∑ k : Fin n, n.choose k / (n - k + 1) * bernoulli' k

and I fear that naively #evaling this in Lean at n=100 will cause B50B_{50}B50​ to be computed 50 times. The loop I wrote in pari avoids this, it only computes every Bernoulli number once. No doubt there is a CS word for this :-)

code

abbrev Frac := Int × Nat

/-! ## Fraction primitives -/

private def simplify : Frac → Frac
  | (_, 0) => (0, 1)
  | (p, q) =>
    let g := Nat.gcd p.natAbs q
    (p / (g : Int), q / g)

private def negF (f : Frac) : Frac := (-f.1, f.2)

private def addF : Frac → Frac → Frac
  | (p1, q1), (p2, q2) =>
    let g   := Nat.gcd q1 q2
    let lcm := q1 / g * q2
    simplify (p1 * ((q2 / g) : Int) + p2 * ((q1 / g) : Int), lcm)

private def mulN (f : Frac) (c : Nat) : Frac :=
  let (p, q) := f
  let g := Nat.gcd c q
  simplify (p * ((c / g) : Int), q / g)

private def divN (f : Frac) (d : Nat) : Frac :=
  let (p, q) := f
  let g := Nat.gcd p.natAbs d
  simplify (p / (g : Int), q * (d / g))

/-! ## Pascal row: [C(n,0), C(n,1), ..., C(n,n)]
    Each step just zips adjacent pairs — O(n) total, no recomputation -/
private def nextPascalRow (row : List Nat) : List Nat :=
  let mid := (row.zip row.tail).map (fun (a, b) => a + b)
  [1] ++ mid ++ [1]

/-! ## Recurrence
    bs.zip row naturally truncates to |bs| pairs (row is always longer) -/
private def nextBernoulli (bs : List Frac) (row : List Nat) : Frac :=
  let k           := bs.length
  let weightedSum := (bs.zip row).foldl (fun acc (bj, cj) => addF acc (mulN bj cj)) (0, 1)
  negF (divN weightedSum (k + 1))

-- Carry the Pascal row as a second accumulator
private def go : Nat → List Frac → List Nat → List Frac
  | 0,     bs, _   => bs
  | n + 1, bs, row => go n (bs ++ [nextBernoulli bs row]) (nextPascalRow row)

-- Seed: bs = [B(0)], row = Pascal row 2 = [C(2,0), C(2,1), C(2,2)]
def bernoulliList (n : Nat) : List Frac := go n [(1, 1)] [1, 2, 1]
def bernoulli     (n : Nat) : Frac      := (bernoulliList n).getLast!

example : bernoulli 9 = (0,1) := by decide
example : bernoulli 18 = (43867, 798) := by rfl
example : bernoulli 20 = (-174611, 330) := by rfl

I have managed to slightly massage @Tomas Skrivan's code to work with cbv for larger instance and to get it to work in approx 3,8s for bernoulli 100 on live.lean-lang.org.

Essentially, I had to register cbv_simprocs for dealing with basic operations on Frac. Moreover, cbv currently doesn't have any specialised simprocs for operations on List , such as append or length, but this is a good argument in favour of having them by default. 

import Lean

abbrev Frac := Int × Nat

/-! ## Fraction primitives -/

private def simplify : Frac → Frac
  | (_, 0) => (0, 1)
  | (p, q) =>
    let g := Nat.gcd p.natAbs q
    (p / (g : Int), q / g)

private def negF (f : Frac) : Frac := (-f.1, f.2)

private def addF : Frac → Frac → Frac
  | (p1, q1), (p2, q2) =>
    let g   := Nat.gcd q1 q2
    let lcm := q1 / g * q2
    simplify (p1 * ((q2 / g) : Int) + p2 * ((q1 / g) : Int), lcm)

private def mulN (f : Frac) (c : Nat) : Frac :=
  let (p, q) := f
  let g := Nat.gcd c q
  simplify (p * ((c / g) : Int), q / g)

private def divN (f : Frac) (d : Nat) : Frac :=
  let (p, q) := f
  let g := Nat.gcd p.natAbs d
  simplify (p / (g : Int), q * (d / g))

/-! ## Simprocs for `Frac` and literal `List` traversal

Without these, every `Frac` op unfolds through a long typeclass chain
(`HMul.hMul → instHMul → Mul.mul → Int.instMul → Int.mul → …`) and `simplify`
rebuilds a `Prod` via pattern matching, and every list traversal walks a
cons-by-cons equation unfolding. The simprocs below extract ground values,
compute the result in meta code, and emit a single-step `Eq.refl`. -/

open Lean Meta Lean.Meta.Tactic.Cbv

namespace CbvBernoulli

/-- Extract an `Int` literal in any canonical form cbv might produce
(`OfNat.ofNat Int k`, `Neg.neg (OfNat.ofNat Int k)`, `Int.ofNat k`, `Int.negSucc k`). -/
def getIntValue? (e : Expr) : OptionT Id Int :=
  match_expr e with
  | Int.ofNat n => do
      let some n := Sym.getNatValue? n | failure
      return (n : Int)
  | Int.negSucc n => do
      let some n := Sym.getNatValue? n | failure
      return Int.negSucc n
  | _ => Sym.getIntValue? e

def getFracValue? (e : Expr) : OptionT Id Frac := do
  let_expr Prod.mk _ _ p q := e | failure
  let p ← getIntValue? p
  let q ← Sym.getNatValue? q
  return (p, q)

def mkFracExpr (f : Frac) : Expr :=
  mkApp4 (mkConst ``Prod.mk [0, 0]) (mkConst ``Int) (mkConst ``Nat)
    (toExpr f.1) (toExpr f.2)

def mkListLit (α : Expr) (u : Level) (xs : Array Expr) : Expr :=
  let nil := mkApp (mkConst ``List.nil [u]) α
  xs.foldr (fun x acc => mkApp3 (mkConst ``List.cons [u]) α x acc) nil

end CbvBernoulli

open CbvBernoulli

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpSimplify (simplify _) := fun e => do
  let_expr simplify a := e | return .rfl
  let some f := getFracValue? a | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (mkFracExpr (simplify f))
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpNegF (negF _) := fun e => do
  let_expr negF a := e | return .rfl
  let some f := getFracValue? a | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (mkFracExpr (negF f))
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpAddF (addF _ _) := fun e => do
  let_expr addF a b := e | return .rfl
  let some f₁ := getFracValue? a | return .rfl
  let some f₂ := getFracValue? b | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (mkFracExpr (addF f₁ f₂))
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpMulN (mulN _ _) := fun e => do
  let_expr mulN a c := e | return .rfl
  let some f := getFracValue? a | return .rfl
  let some c := Sym.getNatValue? c | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (mkFracExpr (mulN f c))
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpDivN (divN _ _) := fun e => do
  let_expr divN a d := e | return .rfl
  let some f := getFracValue? a | return .rfl
  let some d := Sym.getNatValue? d | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (mkFracExpr (divN f d))
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

/-- `xs ++ ys` for literal `List`s → a single literal list. -/
cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpListAppend (@HAppend.hAppend (List _) (List _) (List _) _ _ _) := fun e => do
  let_expr HAppend.hAppend α _ _ _ a b := e | return .rfl
  let_expr List β := α | return .rfl
  let some aElems := getListLitElems a | return .rfl
  let some bElems := getListLitElems b | return .rfl
  let .succ u := (← Sym.getLevel β) | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (mkListLit β u (aElems ++ bElems))
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpListLength (List.length _) := fun e => do
  let_expr List.length _ a := e | return .rfl
  let some elems := getListLitElems a | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (toExpr elems.size)
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpListTail (List.tail _) := fun e => do
  let_expr List.tail α a := e | return .rfl
  let some elems := getListLitElems a | return .rfl
  let .succ u := (← Sym.getLevel α) | return .rfl
  let tail := if elems.size = 0 then elems else elems[1:].toArray
  let result ← Sym.share (mkListLit α u tail)
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpListZipWith (List.zipWith _ _ _) := fun e => do
  let_expr List.zipWith _ _ γ f a b := e | return .rfl
  let some aElems := getListLitElems a | return .rfl
  let some bElems := getListLitElems b | return .rfl
  let k := min aElems.size bElems.size
  let out ← (Array.range k).mapM fun i =>
    Sym.share (mkApp2 f aElems[i]! bElems[i]!)
  let .succ u := (← Sym.getLevel γ) | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (mkListLit γ u out)
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpListZip (List.zip _ _) := fun e => do
  let_expr List.zip α β a b := e | return .rfl
  let some aElems := getListLitElems a | return .rfl
  let some bElems := getListLitElems b | return .rfl
  let k := min aElems.size bElems.size
  let .succ uα := (← Sym.getLevel α) | return .rfl
  let .succ uβ := (← Sym.getLevel β) | return .rfl
  let out ← (Array.range k).mapM fun i =>
    Sym.share (mkApp4 (mkConst ``Prod.mk [uα, uβ]) α β aElems[i]! bElems[i]!)
  let prodT := mkApp2 (mkConst ``Prod [uα, uβ]) α β
  let u := mkLevelMax uα uβ
  let result ← Sym.share (mkListLit prodT u out)
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

cbv_simproc cbv_eval simpListMap (List.map _ _) := fun e => do
  let_expr List.map _ β f a := e | return .rfl
  let some aElems := getListLitElems a | return .rfl
  let out ← aElems.mapM fun x => Sym.share (mkApp f x)
  let .succ u := (← Sym.getLevel β) | return .rfl
  let result ← Sym.share (mkListLit β u out)
  return .step result (← Sym.mkEqRefl result)

/-! ## Pascal row: [C(n,0), C(n,1), ..., C(n,n)]
    Each step just zips adjacent pairs — O(n) total, no recomputation -/
private def nextPascalRow (row : List Nat) : List Nat :=
  let mid := (row.zip row.tail).map (fun (a, b) => a + b)
  [1] ++ mid ++ [1]

/-! ## Recurrence
    bs.zip row naturally truncates to |bs| pairs (row is always longer) -/
private def nextBernoulli (bs : List Frac) (row : List Nat) : Frac :=
  let k           := bs.length
  let weightedSum := (bs.zip row).foldl (fun acc (bj, cj) => addF acc (mulN bj cj)) (0, 1)
  negF (divN weightedSum (k + 1))

-- Carry the Pascal row as a second accumulator
private def go : Nat → List Frac → List Nat → List Frac
  | 0,     bs, _   => bs
  | n + 1, bs, row => go n (bs ++ [nextBernoulli bs row]) (nextPascalRow row)

-- Seed: bs = [B(0)], row = Pascal row 2 = [C(2,0), C(2,1), C(2,2)]
def bernoulliList (n : Nat) : List Frac := go n [(1, 1)] [1, 2, 1]
def bernoulli     (n : Nat) : Frac      := (bernoulliList n).getLast!

example : bernoulli 9 = (0,1) := by cbv
example : bernoulli 18 = (43867, 798) := by cbv
example : bernoulli 20 = (-174611, 330) := by cbv

set_option maxRecDepth 1_000_000_000 in
set_option maxHeartbeats 1_000_000_000 in
set_option cbv.maxSteps 10_000_000 in
example : bernoulli 100 = (-94598037819122125295227433069493721872702841533066936133385696204311395415197247711, 33330) := by cbv

dropping into this thread to mention that one can compute Bernoulli numbers in terms of Euler zigzag numbers, which are naturals, and thereby obtain a fast and easy mostly-rfl proof:

def seidel : Nat → List Nat
  | 0 => [1]
  | n + 1 => (seidel n).reverse.scanr (· + ·) 0

def A (n : Nat) : Nat := (seidel n).head!

def B (n : Nat) : Rat :=
  if n = 0 then 1
  else if n = 1 then 1 / 2
  else if n % 2 = 1 then 0
  else
    let p : Nat := 2 ^ n
    (-1) ^ (n/2 + 1) * (n / (p * (p - 1))) * A (n - 1)

-- about 0.8s on live.lean-lang.org
set_option maxRecDepth 10000 in
theorem A_99 : A 99 = 45608516616801111821043829531451697185581949239892414478770427720660171869441004793654782298700276817088804993740898668991870306963423232 := by
  rfl

example : B 100 = -94598037819122125295227433069493721872702841533066936133385696204311395415197247711 / 33330 := by
  rw [B, show 100 - 1 = 99 by rfl, A_99]
  cbv
(cbv is slower than i had patience for to compute B 100 directly, for whatever reason)

I got a bit nerd-sniped by this, and wondered: What is the most efficient proof term (in terms of kernel checking time, not space – for space Eq.rfl wins always) for calculating bernoulli 100 (without changing the algorithm).

So in a dialogue with Claude I explored this a bit, and ended up with something rather nice. Stats first (row cwp – “compile with proof”)

tactic elab kernel total
native_decide — — 1.3
decide +kernel 1.1 31.3 32.4
cwp 33.0 13.1 46.1
cbv + simprocs 32.5 42.1 74.6
rfl 47.4 31.3 78.7
cbv (vanilla) 87.7 55.7 143.4

how to read the stats

Retired-instruction counts (perf stat -e instructions:u) for a
single-file lake build of each tactic, with both bernoulli 50
and bernoulli 100 proved to literal answers. "elab" measures the
file built with debug.skipKernelTC true; "kernel" is the
difference between +K and −K. Numbers in billions.

The core ideas are:

  • No kernel reduction; an explicit proof term that describes the evaluation of the function and can be checked quickly by the kernel. (Exception: Evaluation of Nat.add etc.)
  • No Eq.trans, Eq.congr or Eq.refl. Instead, for every function we statically generate “per-leaf” equational theorems that assert the function result, with assumptions about the subcalls from the functions. These theorems plug into each other seamlessly (so kernel checking here is structural equality, no real defeq needed).
  • The tactic that evaluates bernoulli 100 and produces the proof term is staged: First all functions involved are compiled into proof-generating variants that do the same computation, on real Int etc, and, on the side, assemble the proof term using these per-leaf equational theorems. Contrast this with approaches like simp, cbv or Meta-rfl, that evaluate bernoulli 100 by, essentially, interpreting the Expr of the original function. I believe this is like mathlib’s norm_num, just not hand-rolled for each function but generated.
  • These generated, compiled functions are specialized to fixed parameters (important for List.map), and partially evaluated (i.e. + turned into Nat.add once and for all).

Concrete example

The simplify function from Test/Bench.lean:

abbrev Frac := Int × Nat

private def simplify : Frac → Frac
  | (p, q) =>
    if q = 0 then (0, 1) else
    let g := Nat.gcd p.natAbs q
    (p / (g : Int), q / g)

run_meta Cwp.Compile.compileFunction ``simplify

compileFunction adds three artifacts to the environment. First,
simplify.cwp — the compiled helper, a real Lean function that
runs as bytecode. Cleaned up (eliding the per-subcall let helperResult := …; let vF := …; let vFLift := …; let helperProof := … boilerplate):

def simplify.cwp : Frac × Lean.Expr → (Frac × Lean.Expr) × Lean.Expr
  | ((p, q), _) =>
    let pLift := Cwp.Native.liftInt p
    let qLift := Cwp.Native.liftNat q
    if q = 0 then
      -- Constant branch: result (0, 1) and its lift are precomputed.
      -- Build a Lean.Expr proof of `qLift = 0` via Decidable.of_decide_eq_true
      -- applied to Eq.refl true (the runtime if-test having just fired the true
      -- branch); pass that Expr as the leaf theorem's path-condition argument.
      let hposExpr : Lean.Expr := mkOfDecideEqTrue (Nat.decEq qLift Nat0Lift)
      ⟨⟨(Int.ofNat 0, 1), mkApp (mkApp Prod.mk Int.ofNat0Lift) Nat1Lift⟩,
       mkApp3 simplify.cwp_eq_leaf_1_pos pLift qLift hposExpr⟩
    else
      -- Thread four subcall triples through, then close with
      -- simplify.cwp_eq_leaf_1_neg.  `hnegExpr` is a Lean.Expr proof of
      -- `qLift ≠ 0`, built analogously via of_decide_eq_false.
      let hnegExpr : Lean.Expr := mkOfDecideEqFalse (Nat.decEq qLift Nat0Lift)
      let ⟨⟨v0, l0⟩, p0⟩ := Int.natAbs.cwp ⟨p, pLift⟩
      let ⟨⟨v1, l1⟩, p1⟩ := Cwp.Native.cwpNatGcd ⟨v0, l0⟩ ⟨q, qLift⟩
      let ⟨⟨v2, l2⟩, p2⟩ := Int.ediv.cwp ⟨p, pLift⟩ ⟨Int.ofNat v1, mkApp Int.ofNat l1⟩
      let ⟨⟨v3, l3⟩, p3⟩ := Cwp.Native.cwpNatDiv ⟨q, qLift⟩ ⟨v1, l1⟩
      let result : Frac := (v2, v3)
      let resultLift := mkApp (mkApp Prod.mk l2) l3
      let proof := mkApp9 simplify.cwp_eq_leaf_1_neg
                          pLift qLift hnegExpr l0 l1 l2 l3 p0 p1 p2 p3
      ⟨⟨result, resultLift⟩, proof⟩

Two leaf theorems are generated, one per ite branch. The negative
branch's leaf bakes in all four subcall results as hypotheses
(rᵢ, hᵢ : <subcall> = rᵢ) so the proof at runtime threads
already-computed values rather than asking the kernel to reduce:

theorem simplify.cwp_eq_leaf_1_neg :
    ∀ (p : Int) (q : Nat), q ≠ 0 →
    ∀ (r1 r2 : Nat) (r3 : Int) (r4 : Nat),
      Int.natAbs p              = r1 →
      Nat.gcd r1 q              = r2 →
      Int.ediv p (Int.ofNat r2) = r3 →
      Nat.div q r2              = r4 →
      simplify (p, q) = (r3, r4)

The positive branch's leaf is the trivial constant case:

theorem simplify.cwp_eq_leaf_1_pos :
    ∀ (p : Int) (q : Nat), q = 0 → simplify (p, q) = (0, 1)

At every consumer call site, the runtime helper computes the four
subcall triples in sequence (each via its own compiled cwp helper),
collects the four lᵢ (lift) and pᵢ (proof Expr) values, and
applies the leaf theorem. No Eq.trans/congrArg chain, no matcher
reference in the proof Expr, no ite reduction by the kernel — the
path condition is in the leaf's binder list and the result-Prod's
lift is constructed by lifting v2 and v3 directly.

Only a PoC, and still tweaking it, so for now just a data point on what would be possible (and how large the gap still is to just unchecked compiled native execution…)

That said, this whole “compiled tactic that produces proof term” is not actually faster than “optimize terms for kernel reduction” in the sense of #5806:

Definitions (rules: no match, no overloaded operators, no recursive def):

  • Nat-recursion (go) via Nat.rec directly.
  • List-recursion (listAppend/Map/Length/Tail/Zip/Foldl/Reverse/Head) via List.rec directly.

  • Prod destructuring via .fst/.snd (structure projections, kernel ι-reduces them in one step
    — not Prod.casesOn).

  • All arithmetic via Nat.add/Nat.mul/Nat.div/Nat.gcd and
    Int.add/Int.mul/Int.ediv/Int.natAbs/Int.ofNat/Int.neg — no +/*/HAdd/OfNat.

  • All defs noncomputable (Lean's bytecode codegen rejects raw .rec bodies; kernel reduces
    them fine).

Statistics:

So:

  • Most of cwp's kernel-cost win (31.3 → 13.1 B vs the standard decide +kernel) is about
    making the kernel's job easier, not about making the proof shorter. Just rewriting the
    definitions in .rec-only form takes the kernel from 31.3 B down to 14.5 B — within ~10 % of
    cwp, with zero proof-construction machinery.

  • cwp keeps a small (~10 %) edge on kernel-only, but pays 33 B in elab to get it. For a
    one-shot proof the reduction-friendly variant wins on total by ≈3× (15.5 vs 46.1 B), beaten
    only by native_decide (which expands the trusted base).

For reference, the kernel-optimized code

/-! # Bernoulli benchmark — reduction-friendly variant

Companion to `Test/Bench.lean` (cwp), `Test/BernoulliRfl.lean` (rfl),
`Test/BernoulliDecideKernel.lean` (decide +kernel on the standard
definitions).  This file exercises the third axis: hand-rolled
definitions deliberately written for the kernel's reduction engine.

Rules:
* No `match` — every destructure goes through `.rec` directly.
* No overloaded operators — `Nat.add a b` not `a + b`, `Nat.mul …`,
  `Int.add …`, etc.  No `OfNat`-style typeclass projections in
  function bodies.
* No recursive `def` — structural recursion uses the inductive's own
  `.rec`; non-structural recursion (here: nothing in the bench) would
  use `Nat.rec` with an explicit fuel arg.

Inspired by leanprover/lean4#5806 — the question is "how cooperative
can the kernel be when the definitions are written for it".  The cwp
row hits 13.1 B retired instructions on kernel TC; we want to know
how close raw kernel reduction can get on the same `bernoulli {50,100}`
proofs given maximally friendly defs.
-/

abbrev Frac : Type := Int × Nat

/-! ## List combinators (no `match`, only `List.rec`).

    Marked `noncomputable` — Lean's bytecode compiler doesn't accept
    raw `.rec` bodies, but the kernel reduces them just fine, which
    is the only path this file exercises. -/

noncomputable def listAppend : List α → List α → List α :=
  fun xs ys => List.rec ys (fun a _ ih => a :: ih) xs

noncomputable def listMap (f : α → β) : List α → List β :=
  List.rec [] (fun a _ ih => f a :: ih)

noncomputable def listLength : List α → Nat :=
  List.rec 0 (fun _ _ ih => Nat.add ih 1)

noncomputable def listTail : List α → List α :=
  List.rec [] (fun _ tail _ => tail)

/-- Zip via nested `List.rec`: outer recursion on `xs`, inner on the
    second arg `ys` inside each cons-arm. -/
noncomputable def listZip : List α → List β → List (α × β) :=
  fun xs =>
    List.rec
      (motive := fun _ => List β → List (α × β))
      (fun _ => [])
      (fun a _ ih ys =>
        List.rec
          (motive := fun _ => List (α × β))
          []
          (fun b bs _ => (a, b) :: ih bs)
          ys)
      xs

noncomputable def listFoldl (f : β → α → β) : β → List α → β :=
  fun init xs =>
    List.rec
      (motive := fun _ => β → β)
      (fun acc => acc)
      (fun a _ ih acc => ih (f acc a))
      xs init

noncomputable def listReverse (xs : List α) : List α :=
  listFoldl (fun acc x => x :: acc) [] xs

/-- Like `List.head!` but with an explicit default — avoids the
    `Inhabited` typeclass projection inside the body. -/
noncomputable def listHead (d : α) : List α → α :=
  List.rec d (fun a _ _ => a)

/-! ## Frac arithmetic — Nat.add/mul/div/gcd, Int.add/mul/ediv/natAbs. -/

@[inline] def fracMk (p : Int) (q : Nat) : Frac := (p, q)
@[inline] def fracP : Frac → Int := Prod.fst
@[inline] def fracQ : Frac → Nat := Prod.snd

noncomputable def negF (f : Frac) : Frac := (Int.neg (fracP f), fracQ f)

/-- Dispatch on `q` via `Nat.rec`: zero arm returns `(0, 1)`, succ arm
    runs the gcd reduction.  No `if`, no `match`. -/
noncomputable def simplify (f : Frac) : Frac :=
  let p := fracP f
  let q := fracQ f
  Nat.rec
    (motive := fun _ => Frac)
    (fracMk (Int.ofNat 0) 1)
    (fun _ _ =>
      let g := Nat.gcd (Int.natAbs p) q
      fracMk (Int.ediv p (Int.ofNat g)) (Nat.div q g))
    q

noncomputable def addF (a b : Frac) : Frac :=
  let p1 := fracP a; let q1 := fracQ a
  let p2 := fracP b; let q2 := fracQ b
  let g   := Nat.gcd q1 q2
  let lcm := Nat.mul (Nat.div q1 g) q2
  simplify
    (fracMk
      (Int.add (Int.mul p1 (Int.ofNat (Nat.div q2 g)))
               (Int.mul p2 (Int.ofNat (Nat.div q1 g))))
      lcm)

noncomputable def mulN (f : Frac) (c : Nat) : Frac :=
  let p := fracP f
  let q := fracQ f
  let g := Nat.gcd c q
  simplify (fracMk (Int.mul p (Int.ofNat (Nat.div c g))) (Nat.div q g))

noncomputable def divN (f : Frac) (d : Nat) : Frac :=
  let p := fracP f
  let q := fracQ f
  let g := Nat.gcd (Int.natAbs p) d
  simplify (fracMk (Int.ediv p (Int.ofNat g)) (Nat.mul q (Nat.div d g)))

/-! ## Pascal-row and Bernoulli iteration. -/

noncomputable def nextPascalRow (row : List Nat) : List Nat :=
  let pairs := listZip row (listTail row)
  let mid := listMap (fun p => Nat.add (Prod.fst p) (Prod.snd p)) pairs
  listAppend (1 :: []) (listAppend mid (1 :: []))

noncomputable def nextBernoulli (bs : List Frac) (row : List Nat) : Frac :=
  let k := listLength bs
  let weightedSum :=
    listFoldl
      (fun acc p => addF acc (mulN (Prod.fst p) (Prod.snd p)))
      (fracMk (Int.ofNat 0) 1)
      (listZip bs row)
  negF (divN weightedSum (Nat.add k 1))

/-- `go` via `Nat.rec` directly — no recursive `def`. -/
noncomputable def go : Nat → List Frac → List Nat → List Frac :=
  Nat.rec
    (motive := fun _ => List Frac → List Nat → List Frac)
    (fun bs _ => bs)
    (fun _ ih bs row =>
      ih (listAppend bs (nextBernoulli bs row :: [])) (nextPascalRow row))

noncomputable def bernoulliList (n : Nat) : List Frac :=
  go n (fracMk (Int.ofNat 1) 1 :: []) (1 :: 2 :: 1 :: [])

noncomputable def bernoulli (n : Nat) : Frac :=
  listHead (fracMk (Int.ofNat 0) 1) (listReverse (bernoulliList n))

/-! ## Proofs.  `decide +kernel` for parity with `Test/BernoulliDecideKernel.lean`. -/

set_option maxRecDepth 1000000000 in
set_option maxHeartbeats 1000000000 in
example : bernoulli 50 = (495057205241079648212477525, 66) := by decide +kernel

set_option maxRecDepth 1000000000 in
set_option maxHeartbeats 1000000000 in
example : bernoulli 100 =
    (-94598037819122125295227433069493721872702841533066936133385696204311395415197247711, 33330)
    := by decide +kernel

Just came across this and FYI, the Isabelle AFP entry on Bernoulli numbers uses the Akiyama–Tanigawa transform to compute Bernoulli numbers, which is not great but better than the naïve approach.

There is also an AFP entry that relates Bernoulli numbers to tangent numbers and provides some reasonably fast (and purely integer-based) algorithms to compute tangent numbers: https://isa-afp.org/entries/Boustrophedon_Transform.html

Neither of these are anywhere near competitive with Harvey's multimodular approach or the Riemann zeta approach, but they are a decent middle ground that requires significantly less work and infrastructure.
